summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It proposes a supposed extra mechanism to ease the move from IPv4 to IPv6 while improving security and privacy. It is humor and not a real specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke proposes security flags for IPv4 and IPv6 packets. It presents made-up rules for marking packets and a fictional privacy flag.

questions: what is the evil bit in ipv4
what is the ipv6 security flag in rfc 8136
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposes security flags for IPv4 and IPv6 packets.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke claims IPv6 lacks an equivalent to the IPv4 security flag described in RFC 3514.
tldr.mechanism: It jokingly requires IPv4 nodes to set that flag and proposes deriving an IPv6 flag from source-address parity, with a second hop-by-hop option as an advanced approach.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational humor document, not a security mechanism to implement.

today: RFC 8136 is an Informational April 1st joke document. It is not a real IPv6 security specification.

sections.title: The Joke's Setup
sections.content:
RFC 8136 is an April 1st joke document. It refers to an Internet Architecture Board statement about future work optimizing for and depending on IPv6, then claims that IPv4 should be marked so network devices can identify it.

The RFC explicitly says its capitalized requirement words are not to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119. Its proposals build on the security flag from RFC 3514.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st RFC jokes about transition from IPv4 to IPv6. It says its requirement words do not have their usual RFC meaning.

sections.title: The Proposed IPv4 and IPv6 Flags
sections.content:
The RFC says all IPv4 nodes must set the RFC 3514 security flag to 1. It then proposes defining an IPv6 security flag as the parity of the source address: an odd number of 1 bits means True; otherwise the flag is False.

As an advanced alternative, it describes a hop-by-hop User Security Flag Option (UFO) with an 8-bit UserSecFlag field. The document says bit 0 carries the security flag and other bits are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The first proposal marks every IPv4 packet. The second uses the number of set bits in an IPv6 source address to determine a flag.

sections.title: The Privacy Extension
sections.content:
The RFC proposes using bit 1 of UserSecFlag as a privacy flag. It says that setting the bit means a packet contains private information and must not be inspected en route, and instructs firewalls, monitoring devices and government agencies to respect it.

The document claims this would need no encryption or key management. These statements are part of the April 1st joke proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The fictional privacy bit asks network devices not to inspect a packet. The proposal claims it needs no encryption or key management.
